findings.title: A flame without an upward direction
findings.claim: NASA's 2015 guide describes microgravity droplet combustion as the textbook case of a spherical droplet surrounded by a spherical flame in a quiescent atmosphere (p. 11); the droplet apparatus used by FLEX handles droplets of 1 to 5 mm (p. 12).
findings.safetyImplication: Treat geometry and ventilation as inputs when translating laboratory observations into spacecraft scenarios.
findings.limitations: Droplet geometry does not represent every solid-material fire or forced-flow condition.

findings.title: Combustion can outlast the visible flame
findings.claim: FLEX experiments discovered non-premixed cool flames aboard the space station in 2012, opening a path to study low-temperature combustion.
findings.safetyImplication: Visible-light appearance alone is an incomplete indicator of combustion state.
findings.limitations: This finding is specific to tested fuels and environments; it does not establish a universal detection threshold.

findings.title: An apparent extinction can be temporary
findings.claim: A NASA Glenn FLEX presentation reports that in space a cool flame can persist after hot-flame extinction and generate combustible vapor that can reignite, that recent results showed re-ignition with decane, and that cool flames could re-ignite to hot flames, posing fire-safety concerns in spacecraft (slide 22 and concluding remarks).
findings.safetyImplication: Post-extinction monitoring should distinguish visual disappearance from demonstrated combustion termination.
findings.limitations: Slide-level statements about droplet tests (decane named); no re-ignition rate, conditions or probability for a crew vehicle are given.

findings.title: Flame spread varied as airflow and oxygen changed
findings.claim: In the published BASS-II PMMA runs, flame-spread rate changed between successive airflow settings while oxygen also fell. In run M3, airflow rose from 10 to 20 cm/s while spread fell from 0.029 to 0.024 mm/s; in run M7, airflow and spread fell together (10 → 3 cm/s, 0.106 → 0.070 mm/s).
findings.safetyImplication: Read airflow and oxygen together: these runs show an association, not an isolated airflow effect.
findings.limitations: Oxygen changed during every run and is reported only as run start and end values; samples also differ in thickness, width and sides burning.

findings.title: Small flames still need multiple diagnostics
findings.claim: Most BASS-II tests had calculated heat-release rates below 100 W, using oxygen consumption and burn duration.
findings.safetyImplication: Include gas measurements alongside heat release when reviewing experimental hazards.
findings.limitations: Small glovebox tests do not represent full-cabin fire consequences.
findings.qualifier: Small glovebox tests, not cabin scale

findings.title: Stopping airflow is not a universal off switch
findings.claim: The Burning Rate Emulator demonstrated combustion lasting minutes without airflow in atmospheres considered for future crew vehicles.
findings.safetyImplication: Do not interpret a zero-ventilation setting as proof of extinction.
findings.limitations: Results concern the tested burner and atmospheres, not every material or cabin.
findings.qualifier: Gas burner emulating solids · tested atmospheres only

findings.title: Bigger flames can lose the heat they need
findings.claim: Flame Design produced quasi-steady spherical non-premixed flames and observed radiative heat loss extinguishing larger flames.
findings.safetyImplication: A visualization should allow extinction; flame size cannot imply monotonically increasing hazard.
findings.limitations: A gaseous-fuel experiment, not a calibrated spacecraft fire model.
findings.qualifier: Gaseous fuel, not a cabin fire model

findings.title: A substantial combustion benchmark collection
findings.claim: NASA reports more than 1,500 ignited flames across six ACME investigations, including flame growth, extinction, soot, and cool-flame studies.
findings.safetyImplication: Use experiment identity and diagnostic method to select comparable evidence.
findings.limitations: A program-wide count is not a count of interchangeable or independently replicated measurements.

findings.title: Material history belongs in the experiment
findings.claim: SoFIE-GEL investigates PMMA-sphere flame growth and extinction as functions of airflow, oxygen percentage, pressure, and internal heating.
findings.safetyImplication: Retain pressure and sample-temperature context when comparing material flammability.
findings.limitations: This record describes investigation objectives, not a reported quantitative outcome.

findings.title: Quiescent does not mean motionless
findings.claim: NASA imagery shows a thin fabric flame brightening periodically in a quiescent microgravity chamber as vaporization-driven flow draws in oxygen.
findings.safetyImplication: A no-fan scenario can still contain fuel-driven transport and changing flame brightness.
findings.limitations: The image sequence does not provide a calibrated temperature or heat-release time series.

findings.title: Exploration atmospheres change the test context
findings.claim: Saffire-VI tested fires in an uncrewed Cygnus spacecraft with elevated oxygen and reduced pressure, using 19 experiment runs.
findings.safetyImplication: Compare oxygen fraction together with pressure when reviewing exploration-cabin evidence.
findings.limitations: The campaign is not a qualification of a particular future cabin or material.
findings.qualifier: Microgravity only · not a cabin qualification

findings.title: The hazard extends beyond the hot zone
findings.claim: Preliminary Saffire results describe substantial combustion-gas hazards despite limited temperature increases away from the fire.
findings.safetyImplication: Present gas exposure and detection timing separately from flame intensity.
findings.limitations: Preliminary test-specific findings; published exposure comparisons are not a universal cabin risk threshold.

findings.title: An enriched atmosphere changes the flame
findings.claim: Saffire-V lowered spacecraft pressure and increased oxygen concentration. NASA reported more energetic flames at elevated oxygen levels and faster burning on thinner PMMA ribs.
findings.safetyImplication: Evaluate atmospheric composition and material geometry together when selecting relevant fire tests.
findings.limitations: Qualitative results from specific Saffire-V conditions do not supply a universal hazard threshold or calibrated intensity function.

findings.title: A detector needs the right smoke signature
findings.claim: SAME was designed to measure smoke particle-size distribution from overheated spacecraft materials in microgravity.
findings.safetyImplication: Detector research should consider the particles produced by relevant materials, as well as flame visibility.
findings.limitations: An investigation objective is not a detector sensitivity result or an alarm threshold.
findings.qualifier: Research objective, not a detector result

findings.title: Test the sensor in the environment it will serve
findings.claim: SAME objectives included evaluating existing spacecraft smoke detectors and advanced detection sensors in microgravity.
findings.safetyImplication: Use detector-specific evidence when comparing detection concepts for crew habitats.
findings.limitations: This overview does not establish a winning sensor design, response time, or operational alarm setting.
findings.qualifier: Research objective, not a detector result

findings.title: Suppression can be studied as a boundary
findings.claim: FLEX was designed to quantify inert-gas suppressant performance and examine the oxygen limit for sustained droplet combustion.
findings.safetyImplication: Extinction evidence needs the fuel, atmosphere, and suppressant context; one limit is not universal.
findings.limitations: A research objective, not an instruction for dosing a suppressant or certifying a crew atmosphere.

findings.title: NASA’s PSI archive has no partial-gravity combustion data yet
findings.claim: The challenge statement (checked November 13, 2026) reports that NASA’s Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) archive currently holds no partial-gravity combustion data. It expects future data from the Lunar-g Combustion Investigation (LUCI) and the Flammability of Materials on the Moon (FM2) experiment. It also suggests that microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity levels.
findings.safetyImplication: Within PSI, Moon and Mars questions rest on microgravity and Earth-gravity results. NASA drop-tower tests published outside PSI found partial-gravity limits below both ends for three materials, so the suggested bounds should be checked against them.
findings.limitations: This describes one archive’s holdings as reported in the challenge statement, not the whole research literature.
findings.qualifier: PSI archive only, per the challenge statement

findings.title: A Moon base atmosphere is likely oxygen-enriched
findings.claim: The challenge statement expects a Moon base and pressurized rovers to use 30% oxygen or more at 10.2 psi or less, between spacesuit conditions (100% oxygen at 4.3 psi) and Earth's atmosphere. It describes this as a more than 40% increase in oxygen concentration that makes materials much more flammable.
findings.safetyImplication: Material flammability evidence gathered near 21% oxygen may not carry over to an exploration habitat; look for tests at elevated oxygen and reduced pressure.
findings.limitations: These are expected design figures quoted in the statement, not a mission specification.
findings.qualifier: Expected design figures, not a specification

findings.title: Gas burners can stand in for solid and liquid materials
findings.claim: ACME's Burning Rate Emulator burns gaseous fuel on a flat porous burner under conditions matched to solid and liquid materials, and measures heat feedback to the burner. NASA describes it as a fire-prevention study that also assesses existing flammability test methods for low and partial gravity.
findings.safetyImplication: Emulation could make screening spacecraft materials faster, if emulated and real materials are shown to behave alike.
findings.limitations: An emulator is a stand-in; this demo has not compared BRE results with tests on real materials.
findings.qualifier: Research objective · emulator not yet validated

findings.title: Electric fields as a stand-in for gravity
findings.claim: E-FIELD Flames applied up to 10,000 volts between a burner and a mesh electrode. The ion wind this produces changes flame shape, soot and stability limits. The challenge statement notes that this mimicked partial gravity through the field's effect on ions in the flame.
findings.safetyImplication: One way existing ISS data touches partial-gravity questions; useful for asking how flame shape changes with an imposed body force.
findings.limitations: An ion-driven force is not buoyancy; NASA states the experiment does not serve space applications directly.

findings.title: The highest-oxygen microgravity flames
findings.claim: According to the challenge statement, ACME's Cool Flames Investigation with Gases (CFI-G) ran the highest-oxygen microgravity tests: oxygen-nitrogen mixtures with up to 85% oxygen flowed from a spherical burner into a chamber of nitrogen and fuel gas such as propane, making an inside-out flame.
findings.safetyImplication: Data near spacesuit and pre-breathe oxygen levels exist only for specific gaseous-flame setups.
findings.limitations: Inside-out gaseous flames do not represent fabrics or plastics burning in a cabin.
findings.qualifier: Gaseous inside-out flames, not cabin materials

findings.title: A smoke instrument reused to measure dust
findings.claim: The challenge statement notes that one instrument used for smoke detection in SAME and SAME-R was used again to detect dust in the Dust and Aerosol Measurement Feasibility Tests (DAFT and DAFT-2).
findings.safetyImplication: Telling smoke from dust is central to avoiding false alarms, especially on dusty lunar surfaces.
findings.limitations: This records instrument reuse; it gives no detector thresholds or false-alarm rates.

findings.title: Inert-gas standards give less margin in low gravity
findings.claim: NASA's 2015 guide reports that FLEX research found the flammability limit with inert-gas suppressants (nitrogen, carbon dioxide, helium or xenon) is lower in reduced gravity, so terrestrial standards for inert-gas suppressants do not offer the same margin of safety (p. 12).
findings.safetyImplication: Suppressant concentrations proven on Earth should not be assumed sufficient in a spacecraft.
findings.limitations: Based on heptane and methanol droplets; other fuels and fire geometries need their own tests.

findings.title: A misdirected suppressant jet can feed a flame
findings.claim: The guide reports early BASS results in which nitrogen applied to a microgravity flame actually strengthened it, because the suppressant stream entrained oxygen. The best point to aim an extinguisher may not be obvious for partly obstructed or wake-stabilized flames (p. 22).
findings.safetyImplication: Extinguisher placement and spray characteristics matter more in microgravity than Earth practice suggests.
findings.limitations: Early, qualitative results from specific BASS tests; no extinguisher design rule follows directly.

findings.title: Three assumptions about spacecraft fire that research overturned
findings.claim: The guide lists three former misconceptions that NASA Glenn research disproved: that a steady fire cannot exist in quiescent microgravity, that a fire will self-extinguish if ventilation is shut off, and that terrestrial fire standards are very conservative because microgravity is inherently safer (p. 35).
findings.safetyImplication: Turning off ventilation is not a guaranteed way to put out a spacecraft fire, and Earth-based flammability tests are not automatically conservative.
findings.limitations: A summary of a research program; specific conditions and materials are in the cited studies.
findings.qualifier: Program summary · details in cited studies

findings.title: Smoke in microgravity looks different to detectors
findings.claim: The guide reports that microgravity research found very different particle sizes in smoke from microgravity flames, so detectors tuned for Earth smoke may look for the wrong signature. A NASA Glenn device that monitors both particles and chemical species outperformed current aircraft smoke detectors in false-alarm rejection and real-event detection in joint FAA testing (p. 35).
findings.safetyImplication: Spacecraft detectors need to be designed for microgravity smoke and should combine particle and gas sensing.
findings.limitations: Test results are summarized, not reported in detail; no thresholds are given here.

findings.title: Ventilated materials may burn as well in orbit as on Earth
findings.claim: BASS tested the hypothesis that materials in microgravity, with adequate ventilation, burn as well as, if not better than, the same material in normal gravity under otherwise identical conditions. The guide also notes spacecraft ventilation airflows of 0 to 30 cm/s (p. 21).
findings.safetyImplication: Normal-gravity flammability ratings may not bound microgravity behavior when air is moving.
findings.limitations: Stated as a hypothesis; results depend on material, thickness, oxygen and flow.

findings.title: FLEX-2 widened droplet tests toward real fuels
findings.claim: NASA's 2015 guide describes FLEX-2 as the follow-on to FLEX, studying mixtures of pure fuels, real-fuel surrogates, soot formation, slow sub-buoyant convective flow and droplet-droplet interactions, with international work on flame spread through droplet arrays and biologically derived fuels (p. 13).
findings.safetyImplication: Moves droplet results closer to practical liquid fuels and to fires involving many droplets, such as sprays or leaks.
findings.limitations: Describes research scope; this demo has not imported FLEX-2 results.

findings.title: Smoke point: when a flame starts to emit soot
findings.claim: The guide reports that SPICE, run in 2009 in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox, studied the transition from non-sooting to sooting gas-jet flames in co-flowing air, aiming at simple predictions of soot emission. The smoke point indicates a fuel's tendency to emit light and soot (p. 13–14).
findings.safetyImplication: Soot and smoke production drive what fire detectors can sense; microgravity soot behavior matters for detection design.
findings.limitations: Gas-jet flames, not burning cabin materials; no SPICE values are imported here.

findings.title: Flames that lift off and restabilize downstream
findings.claim: The guide describes SLICE as studying lifted and lifting flames, where flow and chemistry make a flame detach from the burner and stabilize downstream. It used the SPICE hardware in the glovebox, completed operations in 2012 and preceded ACME's CLD Flame experiment (p. 14–15).
findings.safetyImplication: Shows how airflow changes where and whether a flame anchors, which matters for leaks and ventilated compartments.
findings.limitations: Aimed mainly at cleaner, more efficient burners; fire-safety relevance is indirect.

findings.title: Flames near extinction can pulse for over a minute
findings.claim: The guide reports that near-limit microgravity flames behave very differently from Earth flames, which buoyant flow tends to blow off. A microgravity candle flame oscillated as it depleted nearby oxygen, with growing oscillations that could last over a minute in extreme cases before the flame went out (p. 33).
findings.safetyImplication: A weakening flame in a spacecraft may persist and fluctuate rather than go out at once; detection and post-fire monitoring should allow for this.
findings.limitations: Candle and droplet observations; durations depend strongly on fuel and conditions.
findings.qualifier: Candle and droplet flames · microgravity only

findings.title: A cool flame can keep burning after the visible flame dies
findings.claim: The guide explains that after a large alkane droplet's hot flame went out, the droplet kept vaporizing at the same rate for an extended period, supported by a lower-temperature cool flame that formed after visible extinction. FLEX tests showed the cool flame can burn for a prolonged time (p. 33–34).
findings.safetyImplication: Absence of a visible flame does not mean combustion has stopped; detectors and crews should not rely on sight alone.
findings.limitations: Observed for specific alkane droplets in quiescent microgravity.
findings.qualifier: Alkane droplets in still air only

findings.title: Measured flammability limits at lunar and Martian gravity
findings.claim: In NASA drop-tower tests (Olson & Ferkul, Table I), three materials burned at lower oxygen at lunar and Martian gravity than in microgravity or on Earth. Mylar at 10.2 psia kept burning down to 15.6% oxygen at lunar gravity, against 17.0% in microgravity with 30 cm/s flow and 21.2% at 1 g. Ultem's lunar limit was 21.0% (23.5% at 1 g) and Nomex's 21.0% at 14.7 psia (23.5% at 1 g). NASA's FM2 team notes that such facilities cannot fully reproduce lunar conditions.
findings.safetyImplication: Earth-gravity flammability screening may not be conservative for the Moon or Mars, and microgravity and Earth results did not bound the partial-gravity limits for these materials.
findings.limitations: About 5-second drop-tower tests; reduced-gravity limits are defined differently from 1-g limits; three thin materials; published outside PSI. Lunar and 0g rows come from Ferkul & Olson (2011).

quantities.name: Mylar limiting oxygen at lunar gravity (ULOI*)

findings.title: Large fires measured near exploration-cabin oxygen levels
findings.claim: Saffire VI burned SIBAL cloth at 31.0% oxygen and 54.1 kPa (VI-2), two-sided acrylic (PMMA) at 30.3% and 54.6 kPa (VI-3), and one-sided PMMA at 28.8% and 55.2 kPa (VI-4), all in 20 cm/s concurrent flow in microgravity (Table 1). Peak heat release was 3217 W, 3080 W and 1507 W (Table 2).
findings.safetyImplication: These are the closest measured solid-material fires in the atlas to a lunar-habitat atmosphere, but at lower pressure, forced flow and microgravity.
findings.limitations: Microgravity spacecraft tests at one flow speed; not lunar gravity and not a material qualification.

findings.title: A typical smoke alarm level came late in a real spacecraft fire
findings.claim: During the VI-3 acrylic fire, an ionization smoke detector and a particulate monitor at the far-field unit both responded. Using 1 mg/m³ of particulate as a relatively tight alarm threshold, the authors report that level was reached at 981 s on the Figure 7 time axis, by which point much of the hazardous gas release had occurred.
findings.safetyImplication: Smoke-based alarms may trigger after toxic gases have already spread; detection strategies should consider gas sensing and detector placement.
findings.limitations: One test, one detector location; the 1 mg/m³ threshold is the authors’ chosen level, not the ionization detector’s electrical signal.

findings.title: Gas limits were exceeded while temperatures stayed near normal
findings.claim: In Saffire VI, temperature rose significantly only near the fire, but carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide rose across the spacecraft: both PMMA tests exceeded the 1-hour CO₂ limit and the 24-hour CO limit (VI-3: +8539 ppm CO₂, +308 ppm CO at the far-field unit, Table 2).
findings.safetyImplication: As in terrestrial fires, smoke and gases rather than heat are the main crew hazard; response plans should prioritize gas exposure.
findings.limitations: Concentration increases in a 16.7 m³ free volume; different cabin sizes and ventilation would change exposure.
